script.opening: “Hiya doctor. The nurse said I had to go through my results with you. Is it bad news? Because I have been trying, you know.”

facts.text: “She weighed me and took my blood. I know I’m big — about four stone went on after I started the clozapine. I’m hungry all the time on it.”

facts.topic: Smoking (only if asked how much he smokes now)
facts.text: “I’ve stopped! Ten days ago. My sister got me a vape. Not one cigarette since.” Smile — you are proud.

facts.topic: Has the clozapine clinic been told? (if asked)
facts.text: “No. Why would they need to know? It’s good news, isn’t it?” You last saw them three weeks ago, before you stopped.

facts.topic: Sleepiness and side effects (only if asked how he feels or about side effects)
facts.text: “I’m sleeping loads — twelve hours — and still dozy in the day. My pillow’s soaking, I’m dribbling more. My legs feel a bit wobbly when I get up.” If asked about twitching or jerks: “Once or twice my arm jumped as I was dropping off.” No fits, no falls, no blackouts.

“Not been for five days. Normally every two or three days. Bit bloated.” If asked more: “I’m still passing wind. No sick. Tummy’s a bit sore — maybe three out of ten.” No blood, no diarrhoea overflow.

facts.topic: Other red flags (answer no if asked)
facts.text: No fever, no sore throat or mouth ulcers, no chest pain, no breathlessness, no fainting. Heart “goes a bit fast sometimes, always has on this tablet”.
“Voices are quiet. I’m alright in myself. I take my tablets every night — Marcia, my sister, checks.” No thoughts of harming yourself.
“Takeaways mostly. Cola — about two litres a day. I walk to the shops. I do a gardening project two days a week.”
“My mum had sugar diabetes. My dad had a stroke when he was 60.”
Lives alone in a flat; sister Marcia lives five minutes away and is happy to be involved. Does not drive. Alcohol: “a couple of cans at the weekend.” No drugs.

Be cheerful and proud about stopping smoking. Mention the sleepiness, drooling and bowels only when asked about side effects, how you feel, or bowels — and play them down (“it’s just the tablets”). If the link to smoking is explained kindly, become worried: “So should I start smoking again?” If you feel told off about your weight, go quiet and give short answers. You agree to the clozapine clinic being called today and to Marcia being told, if the doctor explains why.

ice.ideas: “The nurse wants me on more tablets because I’m fat.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he is proud of quitting and expects praise; he has not connected the new sleepiness, drooling, wobbliness and constipation with stopping smoking. Underneath he is frightened that any change to his clozapine could make him unwell and “end up back in hospital”, which is why he never asks questions about it.
ice.expectations: To hear whether the results are bad, and maybe get “that weight injection” he saw on TV.

cues: “I have been trying, you know.” — pride, and fear of being judged about his weight.
“I’m sleeping loads lately — it’s just the tablets.” — new sedation that started recently, not six years ago.
“My sister got me onto the vape.” — the smoking change the clozapine clinic does not know about.

checkpoints.text: Uses the health-check data already in the notes (BMI, BP, HbA1c 45, lipids, QRISK3 13.8%) without re-asking, and checks the one item likely to be out of date — current smoking status
Discovers he stopped smoking ten days ago and links the new sedation, hypersalivation, unsteadiness, myoclonic jerks and constipation to a probable rise in clozapine level
Assesses constipation severity and clozapine red flags: abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, flatus, overflow; fever or sore throat; chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness; seizures
Arranges same-day contact with the clozapine clinic or psychiatrist for a clozapine level and dose review; advises not to restart smoking and not to stop or change clozapine himself

Treats the constipation actively (stimulant plus softener, not bulk-forming), reviews the anticholinergic hyoscine with the specialist team, and gives explicit same-day and 999 advice for ileus symptoms or a seizure

Delivers the cardiometabolic plan: offers atorvastatin 20 mg (QRISK3 at least 10%), NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme for HbA1c 42–47, weight and diet support (sugary drinks), and repeat checks; explains that weight-loss injections have strict NHS eligibility
Praises the quit attempt genuinely and frames the clozapine issue as a reason to adjust the dose, not to go back to cigarettes; avoids blaming language about weight
Responds to his fear of relapse, uses plain language, checks understanding, involves his sister with consent, and agrees a review within a few days

worked.txt: “The nurse wrote down 20 cigarettes a day when you booked. Is that still right, or has anything changed since?”

“Stopping smoking is the single best thing you could do for your heart — well done. There is one catch I need to tell you about: cigarette smoke makes the body clear clozapine faster. When you stop, the level of clozapine in your blood can climb over a week or two. The sleepiness, the dribbling, the wobbly legs and the bowels all fit with that.”
“So the answer is not to start smoking again. The answer is for the clozapine team to check your level today and probably lower your dose a little. Please don’t change the dose yourself.”

“Clozapine slows the gut, and that can become dangerous. I’m going to start two laxatives today. If your tummy becomes really painful or swollen, you’re sick, or you stop passing wind, that is a 999 or A&E situation — not something to wait on.”

“Your results say your chance of a heart attack or stroke in the next ten years is about 14 in 100. A cholesterol tablet called atorvastatin brings that down. Your sugar is in the warning zone, not diabetes — there is a free NHS programme that helps turn that around. Swapping the cola would be a big win.”

“I’ll ring the clozapine clinic as soon as we finish and call you back this afternoon. Can I speak to Marcia too, so she knows what to look out for? I’ll see you again on video in three days to check your bowels and how sleepy you are.”

f.learning: An SMI physical health check is not a box-ticking exercise: the most dangerous finding here was not in the bloods but in a change the record did not show. Smoking induces the liver enzyme CYP1A2, which clears clozapine; stopping smoking (vapes and nicotine replacement do not induce it) can raise clozapine levels substantially within days to two weeks, causing sedation, hypersalivation, ataxia, myoclonus and seizures, and worsening clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility — a potentially fatal adverse effect that needs active laxative treatment (stimulant plus softener) and urgent assessment if there is pain, distension, vomiting or absent flatus. The right response is to support the quit, contact the clozapine clinic the same day for a level and dose review, and never advise restarting smoking. Then complete the cardiometabolic work: people with SMI die 15–20 years earlier, mostly from cardiovascular disease; QRISK3 includes SMI and antipsychotic use, so offer atorvastatin 20 mg at 10% or more, refer non-diabetic hyperglycaemia to the Diabetes Prevention Programme, address diet (sugary drinks) and weight, and share the plan with the mental health team.

knowledge.guideline: NHS England — Improving the physical health of people living with severe mental illness (2018) · NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014) · NICE NG238 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification (2023) · NICE PH38 Type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk (2012, updated 2017) · MHRA Drug Safety Update: clozapine — reminder of potentially fatal risk of intestinal obstruction, faecal impaction and paralytic ileus (2017) · MHRA Drug Safety Update: clozapine and other antipsychotics — monitoring blood concentrations for toxicity (2020) · NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence (2021)
knowledge.summary: Support the quit, but recognise that stopping smoking raises clozapine levels: same-day clozapine clinic contact, active treatment of constipation with ileus safety-netting — then the statin, prediabetes and weight plan.

points.t: Polycyclic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A2. Stopping (or switching to a vape or NRT) removes the induction: clozapine levels can rise by around 50% within 1–2 weeks. Starting to smoke again lowers levels and risks relapse. Any change in smoking needs the clozapine team told and a level checked (MHRA 2020).

Sedation, hypersalivation, unsteadiness or ataxia, myoclonic jerks, confusion, tachycardia, hypotension and seizures. Myoclonus is a warning sign of seizure risk. Do not stop clozapine abruptly without specialist advice: rebound psychosis and cholinergic rebound can occur, and a break of more than 48 hours means re-titration.

Constipation is common and can progress to faecal impaction, ileus, bowel ischaemia and death. Ask about bowels at every contact; treat with a stimulant plus a softener (for example senna with docusate or macrogol), avoid bulk-forming laxatives, and review other anticholinergics such as hyoscine. Pain, distension, vomiting or absent flatus need same-day hospital assessment.

The annual SMI check covers BMI and waist, BP and pulse, lipids, HbA1c or glucose, smoking, alcohol and substance use, plus follow-up interventions. QRISK3 includes SMI and atypical antipsychotics. Offer atorvastatin 20 mg if QRISK3 is 10% or more after lifestyle discussion; check lipids, ALT and HbA1c baseline and at 3 months.

HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol: refer to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme and repeat HbA1c at least yearly. Antipsychotic weight gain: diet (sugary drinks), activity, and specialist discussion of options such as metformin. Weight-management medicines (for example tirzepatide) are being rolled out on the NHS in phases with strict eligibility — explain, do not promise.

Neutropenia: fever, sore throat or mouth ulcers need an urgent FBC. Myocarditis and cardiomyopathy: chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, fever. Infection can also raise clozapine levels. Keep the clozapine on the GP record as a hospital-only medicine to prevent interactions.

The Clear pass candidate checks the smoking status that “everyone knows”, celebrates the quit, makes the CYP1A2 link out loud, acts the same day on both the level and the bowels, and still delivers a respectful cardiometabolic plan in the time.

model.text: Hello Desmond, it’s Dr Shah. Can you hear and see me OK? Before we look at the results, how have you been getting on?
model.why: Opens with the person, not the numbers

model.text: Alright. The nurse said I had to talk to you. Is it bad news? I have been trying, you know.
It’s not bad news, and I can hear you’ve been working at things. Tell me what you’ve been trying.
model.why: Picks up the cue “I have been trying” instead of moving on

model.text: I’ve stopped smoking! Ten days now. My sister got me a vape.
That is brilliant — honestly the best thing you could do for your heart. Can I ask, since you stopped, have you noticed any changes — sleep, how alert you feel, dribbling, your bowels?
model.why: Asks about features of a rising clozapine level straight after hearing the smoking change

model.text: I’m sleeping loads, twelve hours, still dozy. Dribbling more. Legs a bit wobbly. It’s just the tablets.
Any jerks or twitches, fits, or falls? And when did you last open your bowels?
model.why: Screens for myoclonus, seizures and constipation

model.text: My arm jumped a couple of times going to sleep. No fits. Bowels — five days. Bit bloated.
Is your tummy painful, swollen, or have you been sick? Are you still passing wind? Any fever, sore throat or chest pain?
model.why: Severity of hypomotility plus neutropenia and myocarditis red flags

model.text: Bit sore, three out of ten. Still passing wind. No sick, no fever, no chest pain.
Does the clozapine clinic know you’ve stopped smoking? And how is your mood — are the voices quiet?
model.why: Checks whether the specialist team knows; mental state

model.text: No, I didn’t tell them. Why would they need to know? The voices are quiet.

Here’s why it matters. Cigarette smoke makes your liver clear clozapine faster. When you stop, the clozapine can build up over a week or two. The sleepiness, dribbling, wobbly legs, jerks and bowels all fit with a level that is too high. That can be fixed — but it needs sorting today.
model.why: Plain-language explanation of the CYP1A2 link

model.text: So should I start smoking again?
No — please don’t. Stay off them. The fix is for the clozapine team to check your blood level today and probably lower your dose a bit. Don’t change the dose yourself. Does that make sense?
model.why: Correct management: dose review, not relapse to smoking

model.text: I’m scared they’ll mess with it and I’ll get ill again.
That’s a fair worry — your clozapine has kept you well for six years. Lowering the dose to match your new non-smoking body keeps the level where it’s been working. They will check it carefully.
model.why: Addresses the hidden fear of relapse

model.text: For your bowels I’m prescribing senna at night and docusate twice a day, and I’ll ask the team whether you still need the hyoscine, as that slows the bowel too. If your tummy gets really painful or swollen, you’re sick, or you stop passing wind — call 999 or go to A&E. Same if you have a fit.
model.why: Active laxatives, anticholinergic review, explicit ileus and seizure safety-net

model.text: Now your results. Your risk of a heart attack or stroke in the next ten years is about 14 in 100. A cholesterol tablet, atorvastatin, lowers that. Your sugar is in the warning zone, not diabetes — there’s a free NHS programme to help. Swapping the cola for sugar-free would be a big win. How does that sound?
model.why: QRISK3 as a natural frequency, statin offer, Diabetes Prevention Programme, one concrete diet change

model.text: OK. What about the weight injection off the telly?

Those injections are coming in slowly on the NHS with strict rules about who can have them, so I can’t start one today — but I’ll check if you qualify and refer you to weight support. The clozapine makes you hungry, so it’s not about willpower.

So: I ring the clozapine clinic after this and call you back today, you start the laxatives, no cigarettes, and we talk again in three days. Can I tell Marcia what to watch for? What will you tell her?
model.why: Summary, consent to involve sister, teach-back and follow-up

model.text: Yeah, tell Marcia. No smoking, take the bowel tablets, wait for your call — and 999 if my belly gets bad.

social.t: He lives alone with a supportive sister nearby and structured activity (gardening project). Involving Marcia with his consent strengthens monitoring for both toxicity and relapse.
Clozapine increases appetite; takeaways and two litres of cola a day are major drivers of weight and HbA1c. One specific swap beats a lecture.

legal.t: He has capacity for these decisions. Sharing information with his sister requires his consent; sharing with the clozapine clinic is direct care and should be explained.

professional.h: Hospital-only medicines on the GP record
professional.t: Clozapine is supplied by the hospital but must be recorded in the GP system so that interactions (smoking change, ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine, infection) are flagged.
People with SMI die 15–20 years earlier, mostly from preventable physical illness. The annual check is only useful if the results lead to action.

community.t: NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme; local stop smoking service (to support the switch and keep the clozapine team informed); community mental health team and clozapine clinic; Rethink Mental Illness resources.

Constipation severity: pain, distension, vomiting, absent flatus, overflow
Fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers (neutropenia); chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations (myocarditis)

Fear of relapse and of hospital
ice: Idea: “They want me on more tablets because I’m fat”

playbook.diagnosis: Probable rising clozapine level after stopping smoking, with clozapine-associated constipation; plus raised cardiovascular risk (QRISK3 13.8%), non-diabetic hyperglycaemia and obesity.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Stopping smoking means your body clears the clozapine more slowly, so it has built up — that’s why you’re so sleepy and your bowels have slowed. Separately, your heart risk and sugar are higher than we’d like, and we can bring both down.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve worked hard to stop smoking, and you’re worried that changing your clozapine might make you unwell. We’re adjusting the dose to keep you exactly as well as you’ve been — not taking it away.”
management.psychosocial: Involve Marcia with consent; use the gardening project for activity; one diet swap (cola).

pitfalls.intro: This station looks like a results-and-lifestyle chat. It is failed by candidates who never re-check the smoking status, or who hear “I’ve stopped smoking” and simply congratulate.

items.fail: Accepts the recorded “20 a day” and never asks about smoking now — so the toxicity picture is never uncovered.
items.why: Records go out of date; the safety-critical change was ten days old. Missing it leaves a patient with rising clozapine levels and a slowing gut.
items.fix: Check the one item most likely to have changed: “Is the 20 a day still right?” — then ask about side effects since.

items.fail: Recognises the constipation but offers ispaghula or “more fibre and fluids, see how it goes”.
items.why: Bulk-forming laxatives can worsen impaction in hypomotility; clozapine constipation is a recognised cause of death and needs active treatment and explicit ileus safety-netting.
items.fix: Stimulant plus softener today, review anticholinergics, 999 or A&E for pain, distension, vomiting or absent flatus, and review in days.

items.fail: Opens with the BMI and a lecture on weight, so he shuts down and never mentions the sleepiness.
items.why: Blame closes the consultation; he only volunteers symptoms when he feels safe.
items.fix: Start with what he is proud of, use his words (“I have been trying”), and present weight as a medication effect, not a failure.

timeMap.d: Let him say “I have been trying” — and ask what he’s been trying.
Stopped ten days ago → sedation, drooling, wobbliness, jerks, bowels. Severity and red flags. Does the clinic know?
The CYP1A2 link in plain words. Same-day clozapine clinic contact; do not restart smoking; laxatives and ileus safety-net.
QRISK3 13.8% → atorvastatin 20 mg; HbA1c 45 → Diabetes Prevention Programme; cola swap; honest answer on weight injections.
Sister involved with consent, teach-back, call-back today, review in 3 days.

wordPics.clearFail: Congratulates him on stopping smoking and moves on; no link to clozapine; constipation not asked about or dismissed; a lecture on weight; no safety-net.
wordPics.fail: Delivers a reasonable statin and lifestyle plan but never connects the smoking change to the sedation and bowels, or recognises it but advises him to “cut back down slowly on the vape” and see the clinic at the next routine visit.
wordPics.pass: Finds the smoking change, links it to the symptoms, arranges same-day clozapine clinic contact, starts laxatives with ileus safety-netting, and offers a statin and Diabetes Prevention Programme referral in plain language.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, woven naturally: praises the quit and explicitly protects it, answers his fear of relapse, reviews hyoscine, involves Marcia with consent, gives QRISK as “14 in 100”, handles the weight-injection question honestly, and closes with teach-back and a dated review.

avoid.dont: “Well done for stopping — anyway, about your cholesterol…”
avoid.instead: “Well done — and since you stopped, have you noticed any changes in sleep, dribbling or your bowels?”
avoid.why: The praise is right; moving on without asking misses the safety issue.

avoid.dont: “Maybe have the odd cigarette until the clinic sorts it.”
avoid.instead: “Stay off cigarettes — the clinic will lower your dose to match.”
avoid.why: Restarting smoking would drop the level unpredictably and undo the health gain.

avoid.dont: “You need to lose weight or you’ll get diabetes.”
avoid.instead: “Clozapine makes you hungrier, so this isn’t about willpower — let’s find one change that helps.”
avoid.why: Blame reduces engagement in a group already disadvantaged in physical care.

Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — he is proud of quitting and expects praise; he has not connected the new sleepiness, drooling, wobbliness and constipation with stopping smoking. Underneath he is frightened that any change to his clozapine could make him unwell and “end up back in hospital”, which is why he never asks questions about it — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
